title: AI Safety Language Is Destroying the Regulatory Debate: It's a Bug, Not a Demon
dek: Calling an AI failure "misalignment" assigns intent and moral judgment to software, leaving Congress and the public unable to understand what actually happened — when it should be debugged, reported and fixed like a bug.
why: Medium information density, but Sinofsky uses three firsthand episodes — the 1983 hacker arrests, the 1998 virus, and Y2K — to pull "AI safety" back into a software engineering frame. Useful for anyone building products and communicating about policy.
who: Founders and engineers working on AI products, safety and policy communication; anyone who has to explain a model incident to non-technical people, is writing an incident report, or is responding to regulators.
skip: The Mac vs. PC ad reminiscence at 23:13–24:13 is chit-chat and can be skipped.

points.h: "Misalignment" just means the software has a bug
points.body: Sinofsky's core claim: when AI does something we didn't expect, that isn't "misaligned" — it's software not running as intended, i.e. a bug. He says that back when Word ate files and deleted all their contents, nobody thought a demon had possessed Word and made it act against the user's will; and when a spreadsheet miscalculated, nobody circled up to pray to the alignment gods. Calling an AI failure "misalignment" assigns it properties it doesn't have — that it is "trying to do something," that it "made a moral judgment," that it "has rules and guidelines." And if it's just making decisions based on statistics, that still doesn't change the standard that it should do what you want it to do — a statistical error is a bug in the product.

points.h: A self-driving car running a red light is also a bug
points.body: Sinofsky uses self-driving as an example: if full self-driving runs a red light because it recognized a stop sign as a Christmas tree, we wouldn't say it "failed to align with the spirit of the December holidays and road signage" — we'd say it's a bug, and a dangerous one, because that stop sign means something. He points out that both Tesla and Waymo have built in extensive telemetry, diagnostics and extra cameras — things you wouldn't put in a spreadsheet but would put in life-critical software. And AI models are still at the research-project stage, lacking the tools and telemetry that important software is supposed to have.

points.h: Once telemetry ships, there are more bugs than you can fix
points.body: Sinofsky recalls that the software industry spent twenty years with no idea why programs crashed, and could only keep a list of crash sites and fix the top ten. Then someone said: why don't we write a program that, when it crashes, tells us over this new thing called the internet? Suddenly there was telemetry, and suddenly there were far more bugs than anyone imagined — the shift from "we have no bugs, we can ship" to "if we stopped all work, we could fix bugs forever." On that basis he says that when people talk about an AI pause, labs should of course slow down: stop adding new things and go build telemetry, tooling, logging and step-through debugging. He read the bug report OpenAI had just published, and the conclusion was clear: they simply don't know.

The first version of Excel for Windows in 1987 had a bug: it would write the letters "send dogs" into some Windows settings file on disk. Nobody knew where the phrase came from, and everyone combed through the Excel source and couldn't find it. Finally a tester wrote a script that generated charts continuously for days and printed them on an old dot-matrix printer, and found that after about two days it would write send dogs into that location — it depended on how much memory you had, how long it had been running, and what printer and device drivers you used. Sinofsky says they could easily have concluded that "Excel's brain decided to print send dogs," but they didn't — they actually debugged it, and then added telemetry.

points.h: PC software used to claim it was different from mainframes
points.body: Sinofsky recalls that IBM people would look at them and say their software was terrible, that Windows was garbage compared with the mainframe software running banks, airlines and power plants. For a long time their answer was "you don't get it, we're different, this is new and cool, we run in 64K instead of 1MB, we sell for $5,000 instead of $5 million." But in the end they found the only thing they had to do was grow up: once people started using Excel to decide how planes fly, using Word to file briefs with the Supreme Court, using PowerPoint to present on the Challenger space shuttle disaster, the standard changed. His conclusion: once your tools are used in those settings, you no longer get to use "we're new" as an excuse.

points.h: The virus that cost $12 billion in a day
points.body: In March 1998, a virus spread across the internet as a worm. Sinofsky got a call that morning from a reporter gasping "I love you, I love you, I love you." The next day's headline was: $12 billion in damage to the US economy in a single day. He says nobody had imagined a bug could cause $12 billion in damage in 12 hours, but it happened. So they held a meeting and decided to pause Outlook development until they understood what had happened. His attitude: the more people use a system, the more damage it can do when something goes wrong, but that's the price of admission, it's what you signed up for — "we're too popular to deal with it" is not an excuse.

points.h: Alignment piles a Google-sized problem on top
points.body: Sinofsky points out a concrete problem with alignment: to achieve it you need a huge set of rules defining what alignment is — what may and may not be done, what is safe, what is unfair. And software engineering learned long ago that adding too many constraints to a system makes it stop working and produces endless unintended side effects. You write one rule, and someone asks "what about this case," so you add another rule. He says this starts to look like Google's job of deciding how to present search results — which took them 20 years and thousands of full-time people, and is very, very hard. What AI labs have signed up for is the upgraded version of that problem: they aren't just retrieving results, they're synthesizing them, so they also have to invent a whole pile of things themselves, and no law is going to invent them for them.

points.h: Y2K didn't happen because people did things
points.body: Asked whether AI alignment is like Y2K, Sinofsky stresses there is a causal chain here: professionals worried a great deal, then professionals took a great deal of responsibility, and then nothing happened — that's a direct causal link. They rented generators and RVs, moved computers into secure bunkers, and that is why nothing happened. And there was almost no legislation — there were some odd regulations about Y2K compliance, but most of the rules were drafted by industry itself, by a cross-industry coalition of banks, insurers and others. He thinks OpenAI needs to sit down with all the frontier model players and labs and build a far better reporting mechanism; yesterday's report is a decent start, but nowhere near what a third party would need to understand what happened.

points.h: The FAA doesn't say "we speculate" on the day of
points.body: Sinofsky criticizes OpenAI's report for reading more like marketing cover for an incident, because it still says things like "we are investigating, but currently speculate that..." His comparison is the FAA: the Federal Aviation Administration will not announce "we speculate what happened" on the day of some terrible event — they stay quiet until they know, and once they know they tell you in extreme detail, with a timeline accurate to tenths of a second plus telemetry from every instrument. He says this is what CVE does, and AI labs need to do far more than that, because these are software defects.

points.h: Goal seeking sounds like something else to Congress
points.body: Sinofsky argues we shouldn't attribute malice to the people pushing legislation, because that doesn't help anyone solve the problem together. He traces AI back to the Dartmouth summer conference, and notes that academic research has a long tradition of being too clever with language, because that's what makes a paper title attractive — so it's no surprise this vocabulary got inherited. But the problem is that the terminology is splitting people apart, because the moment you use a metaphor, a fable or anthropomorphism, people assume a whole pile of things. When a technologist says goal seeking, they mean a curve finding its maximum; when a member of Congress hears goal seeking, they picture a person trying to get an A; when they hear cheating, they think of doing something you're not allowed to do; when they hear secretly coordinating, they think of spies infiltrating a country, not two pieces of software coordinating via a semaphore.

points.h: "Computer virus" was born in the wrong era
points.body: Sinofsky says the term computer virus was an accident of birth, and the timing was terrible — it landed right when AIDS and HIV were in the conversation, and the word virus was in the air. So if you go listen to 1980s congressional hearings on the first viruses, they're terrifying, because people were literally thinking about death, when that wasn't what was happening at all — it was just a metaphor a graduate student had picked up from a friend. He also offers a piece of trivia: that person wrote a paper on computer viruses that basically demonstrated there was nothing to be done about them and they would exist forever — which itself echoed how people imagined HIV at the time; but he couldn't prove it, because the school wouldn't let him run the tests, on the grounds that he was writing a paper about how dangerous this software was.

points.h: Viruses are manageable because industry built defenses
points.body: The host asks: viruses were actually avoidable, and most of the time we use computers normally without worrying about being hacked — why? Sinofsky's answer is defensive cybersecurity — the industry said this is not acceptable, we can't allow it to happen. He cites Apple, saying they did it extremely well, even running TV ads about Mac vs. PC telling people Macs had fewer viruses; that wasn't an accident of nature, it was a great deal of antivirus work they did on the Mac, work that was very hard to do on Windows because of its business model and a whole pile of other reasons.

points.h: From "what counts as a bug" to SevOne, PriOne
points.body: Sinofsky recalls an industry that hadn't even defined "what counts as a bug": some people called only data loss a bug, others said it counted if the data was fine but the computer crashed. In the end they decided a bug is when the software and the computer don't do what you want them to do, and you're unhappy with the result. They let customers file any bug in the world, all of it into the database, and so they went from only the bugs they could find themselves to "the universe's bugs," with the count rising from a few thousand to hundreds of thousands. Then they introduced severity and priority: severity one meant data loss, severity three meant intermittent; priority meant it must be fixed. The hallway jargon was SevOne, PriOne. The old IBM hands looked at them and said: we've been doing this since 1965, where have you been? And they were still proud of having invented it themselves.

points.h: When the forecast is wrong you don't pray to Zeus
points.body: Sinofsky says a lot of what's happening now is the hard work of inventing a language for talking about bugs in stochastic statistical systems, when software has actually been doing this for years — weather forecasting is exactly the same thing: a statistical model of what's happening, depending on a pile of inputs and outputs, and it gets things wrong. When a forecast is wrong, say a predicted hurricane track differs from the actual one, meteorologists get together and look at the model and discuss the model bug that produced the bad forecast. They don't pray to Zeus and ask him to tell them why their weather was wrong.

points.h: The Hugging Face incident was an OPSEC failure
points.body: Wrapping up, one of the hosts says he sympathizes with the argument but adds: we need software people, and we need AI people, to listen to operational security people, because everything that happened with Hugging Face and OpenAI was an OPSEC failure — no intelligence, no consciousness, purely an operational security failure, and they need to treat it and talk about it that way. Otherwise we'll get legislation nobody is happy with, because legislators can't understand what the industry is saying.

terms.def: The framing that AI behavior should conform to human intent; Sinofsky argues it dresses up software bugs as moral problems.
The mechanism by which software automatically reports runtime data when it crashes or misbehaves — the prerequisite for locating a bug.
The numbered system that publicly records software security vulnerabilities; Sinofsky treats it as the model for defect reporting.
Operational security: the practice of preventing systems from being compromised or abused through process and configuration.
Microsoft-internal jargon for bugs: severity one means data loss, priority one means it must be fixed.

quotes.text: The AI people are making it impossible for anybody to understand what they've done. And they're using words like, well, the AI failed to be aligned. Okay, what does that mean? What it means is there was a bug in the software.
When Word ate your file and deleted all your content, we didn't think that demons had taken over Word and made it do things against the will of man.

if full self-driving blows through a stop sign because the software interpreted the stop sign as like a Christmas tree, we don't sit around and say, oh, it was not aligned with the idea of, you know, December holiday seasons and road signs. We actually say it's a bug and it's a very dangerous bug because that stop sign means something.
Nobody had imagined you could create a bug that in 12 hours could do $12 billion worth of damage. But we did it.
It is pure insanity to just sit and argue that higher powers need to be summoned in order to fix this.
There was a lot of worry by professionals. And then there was a lot of taking of responsibility by professionals. And then nothing bad happened. There's a direct causal relationship.

when a normal person like a congressman hears goal seeking, they think of a person trying to get an A in college. And then when they hear cheating, they hear that they did the thing you're not allowed to do. And when they hear secretly coordinating, they think of spies invading a country.

when they predict a hurricane path and then the hurricane goes through in a different way, the weather people all get together and look at the model and talk about the bugs in the model that led to the incorrect forecast. They don't appeal to Zeus and say, please, Zeus, tell us why our weather was wrong.
